key_insight: Selective Chain-of-Thought (Selective CoT) first predicts whether a medical question needs step-by-step reasoning and only generates a rationale when required, preserving answer accuracy while reducing unnecessary compute and latency.
problem_solved: LLMs waste time and compute by producing chain-of-thought explanations for every medical question, even when many questions can be answered directly; this approach avoids unnecessary reasoning without degrading performance.
method: Use an inference-time classifier to predict if a question requires chain-of-thought reasoning.
Conditionally generate a detailed rationale only for questions flagged as needing reasoning; otherwise output a direct answer.
Evaluate the strategy with open-source LLMs (Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen-2.5-7B) on biomedical QA benchmarks (e.g., HeadQA, MedQA-USMLE, MedMCQA, etc.) to measure accuracy vs. efficiency trade-offs.
impact: Enables more efficient, lower-latency deployment of LLMs in medical QA by cutting needless reasoning steps while maintaining clinical-grade accuracy—important for scalable, cost-sensitive healthcare applications.
visual_elements: Flowchart showing: Input question → Classifier (Needs reasoning? Yes/No) → {Generate CoT + Answer | Direct Answer}
Bar chart comparing accuracy, latency, and token/compute usage for Always-CoT vs Selective CoT
Before/after example QA pair: one requiring CoT (with rationale) and one solved directly, annotated to highlight differences
Savings infographic (icon + % compute/time saved) to emphasize efficiency gains
paper_title: To Reason or Not to: Selective Chain-of-Thought in Medical Question Answering
paper_authors: Zaifu Zhan, Min Zeng, Shuang Zhou, Yiran Song, Xiaoyi Chen
